title: Lazy Initialization Pattern
oneLiner: Delays creating an object until the exact moment it's first actually needed.

hero.name: The Procrastinator
hero.catchphrase: Why build it now if nobody's asked for it yet?
hero.power: Defers expensive construction until the first real access, so unused objects never cost anything.
hero.weakness: Whoever triggers the first access unexpectedly pays the full construction cost — and in multi-threaded code, two threads can race to initialize at once if it's not synchronized.
hero.origin: The Procrastinator appeared after an app's startup time ballooned to 8 seconds because every feature module eagerly loaded its data on boot, whether the user ever opened that feature or not.

story.problem: App startup eagerly constructs every feature module's data — including the rarely-used 'export to legacy format' module — adding seconds to every launch, whether or not the user ever touches it.
story.solution: The Procrastinator wraps the expensive module in a lazy accessor. The module isn't constructed until the very first time something actually calls `getLegacyExporter()`.
story.result: Startup time drops because unused modules are never built at all. The one time a user does need legacy export, it initializes on the spot.

before: Every module is constructed eagerly at startup
Rarely-used features cost startup time for everyone
Startup time scales with total feature count, not usage
after: Modules construct only on first actual use
Rarely-used features cost nothing until touched
Startup time scales with what's actually used, not total features

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A startup profiler shows 8 seconds spent constructing twenty feature modules, most never opened.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're building the legacy exporter on every single launch, and maybe one user in a thousand ever touches it.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Procrastinator appears, yawning, refusing to build anything until someone actually asks.
panels.speaker: The Procrastinator
panels.dialogue: Why build it now? Wait until someone actually calls for it. Most of these modules will never be asked for at all.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: getLegacyExporter() checks if the instance exists; if not, it builds it right then, on first access.
panels.speaker: The Procrastinator
panels.dialogue: The first caller pays the construction cost. Everyone before that pays nothing at all.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Startup drops to under a second. The legacy exporter builds itself the one time someone actually needs it.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Startup went from 8 seconds to under 1. The features nobody uses now cost nobody anything.

useWhen: An object is expensive to create but only sometimes (or rarely) actually used.
You want to reduce startup time by deferring non-essential initialization.
The cost of checking 'has this been created yet?' is much cheaper than construction itself.
avoidWhen: The object is cheap to construct — laziness adds a branch for no real savings.
The object is virtually always used anyway, so deferring it just adds complexity with no benefit.
Multiple threads might trigger first access simultaneously without proper synchronization, risking a race condition.
commonMistakes: Forgetting synchronization in multi-threaded environments, letting two threads both see 'not yet created' and construct two instances.
Making an object lazy that's needed almost immediately anyway — the deferred cost doesn't actually move, it just gets paid at an unpredictable moment.
Hiding a very expensive first-access cost behind an innocent-looking getter, surprising callers with unexpected latency.
Confusing Lazy Initialization with Singleton — they're often combined (a lazily-created single instance), but they solve different problems.
explanation.realWorldExample: Lazily-loaded database connections, lazy image loading in web pages (`loading="lazy"`), and framework dependency injection containers that construct services on first request rather than at startup are all Lazy Initialization.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this basically how Singleton's getInstance() already works?

conversation.speaker: The Procrastinator
conversation.message: Often, yes — Singleton frequently uses me under the hood. But I'm a broader idea: ANY expensive value can be deferred this way, not just single shared instances.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What goes wrong if I'm careless?

conversation.speaker: The Procrastinator
conversation.message: Multi-threaded races. Two threads can both check 'not built yet' at the same instant and both build it — you need proper synchronization, or you'll get two instances where you expected exactly one.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app's settings screen has a rarely-visited 'Advanced Diagnostics' panel that loads 50MB of debug tooling data on every app launch, even though fewer than 1% of users ever open it.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Procrastinator defers loading the 50MB of diagnostics data until the user actually opens that panel, keeping app launch fast for everyone else.

quiz.question: What does Lazy Initialization primarily save?
options: The cost of constructing objects that end up never being used
Memory used by objects that are already in active use
Disk space on the user's device
quiz.answer: The cost of constructing objects that end up never being used
quiz.explanation: By deferring construction until first use, objects that are never touched never cost anything at all.

quiz.question: What's the classic multi-threaded bug risk with Lazy Initialization?
options: Two threads can both see 'not yet created' at the same time and construct two separate instances
It always causes a memory leak
It prevents the object from ever being garbage collected
It requires a database connection to function
quiz.answer: Two threads can both see 'not yet created' at the same time and construct two separate instances
quiz.explanation: Without synchronization, the check-then-create sequence isn't atomic across threads, creating a race condition.

quiz.question: When is Lazy Initialization unnecessary?
options: When the object is cheap to construct or is used almost every time regardless
When the object is expensive and rarely used
When startup time is a measured concern
When most users never touch the feature the object supports
quiz.answer: When the object is cheap to construct or is used almost every time regardless
quiz.explanation: If construction is cheap, or the object is needed anyway, deferring it adds complexity without meaningful savings.

quiz.question: How does Lazy Initialization commonly relate to Singleton?
options: Singleton's getInstance() often uses lazy initialization internally to defer creating the single instance until first requested
They are mutually exclusive and can never be combined
Lazy Initialization requires multiple instances to exist
Singleton always initializes eagerly and never lazily
quiz.answer: Singleton's getInstance() often uses lazy initialization internally to defer creating the single instance until first requested
quiz.explanation: The two patterns are frequently combined: a Singleton whose single instance is created lazily on first access.
